title: AVL Tree
summary: An AVL tree is a self-balancing binary search tree that keeps every node's balance factor within −1, 0, or +1. After each insert or delete, single or double rotations restore O(log n) height.
objectives: Students can compute the height and balance factor of every node in a binary search tree.
Students can identify which of the four AVL rotation cases (LL, RR, LR, RL) repairs an unbalanced node.
Students can trace insert and delete on an AVL tree, including bottom-up height updates and rotations.
Students can explain why AVL trees guarantee O(log n) search, insert, and delete in the worst case.
Students can compare single rotations with double rotations and explain why delete may trigger more than one rotation.

beginner: Think of a hanging mobile with weights on two arms: if one side grows much longer than the other, the mobile tips over. An AVL tree is a binary search tree that refuses to tip. It keeps every left subtree and right subtree nearly the same height so searches never degrade into a long chain.

Every node tracks its height: the number of edges on the longest path down to a leaf. A leaf has height 0, and an empty child counts as −1. Each node also has a balance factor: left subtree height minus right subtree height. In an AVL tree, every balance factor must stay −1, 0, or +1.

When you insert or delete a key, the tree first updates just like a regular binary search tree. Then it walks back up toward the root, updating heights. If any node reaches a balance factor of +2 or −2, the tree fixes that spot with a rotation: a quick pointer rearrangement that keeps all keys in sorted order.

Named after inventors Adelson-Velsky and Landis, an AVL tree handles four imbalance patterns: Left-Left (LL), Right-Right (RR), Left-Right (LR), and Right-Left (RL). LL and RR need one single rotation; LR and RL straighten a kink first, using two rotations.
intermediate: Each AVLNode in src/structures/avl.js stores id, value, left, right, and height, with a default capacity of 31 unique integers. The page displays each node's height (h) and balance factor (bf = h(left) − h(right)) right under the circle and marks any node with |bf| = 2 with a thick ring and a ! suffix.

Insert checks that the key is not already present before reporting overflow, walks down from the root (rejecting duplicates), and attaches a new leaf with height 0. It then retraces the recorded ancestor path bottom-up. At each ancestor, height becomes 1 + max(h(left), h(right)) and bf is checked.

If bf = +2, the node is left-heavy: child bf ≥ 0 is an LL case (one right rotation around the node), while child bf < 0 is an LR case (rotate the left child left, then rotate the node right). Symmetrically, bf = −2 triggers RR (one left rotation) when right child bf ≤ 0, or RL (right on the child, left on the node) when right child bf > 0.

Delete removes a leaf or promotes a single child; for a node with two children, it copies the in-order successor's key into the target node and unlinks the successor. Retracing walks up from the removal point and stops early as soon as a subtree's height matches its old height, since no higher ancestor can be affected.

Every rotation re-links three pointers and recomputes two heights in O(1) time. Because strict balance keeps tree height logarithmic, search, insert, delete, min, and max all run in O(log n) worst-case time, while reading the root's stored height takes O(1).
advanced: The minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h follows the Fibonacci-like recurrence N(h) = N(h − 1) + N(h − 2) + 1 with N(0) = 1 and N(1) = 2. Solving this yields h < 1.44·log₂(n + 2), tighter than a red-black tree's 2·log₂(n + 1) bound.

After an insert, the first single or double rotation always restores the unbalanced subtree to its pre-insert height, so at most one rotation case occurs per insert. After a delete, a rotation can reduce the subtree's height by 1, which can unbalance a higher ancestor and cause up to O(log n) rotations up to the root.

Compared with red-black trees, AVL trees give slightly faster lookups because they are shorter, at the cost of extra rotations during frequent insertions and deletions. They also store an integer height (or 2-bit balance factor) per node instead of a 1-bit color.

This implementation keeps no parent pointers: insert and delete record ancestors in a path array of O(log n) space. It uses the edge-count height convention (empty −1, leaf 0) rather than node-count (empty 0, leaf 1), and two-child deletion copies the successor's value into the existing node so node ids stay stable during SVG gliding.

pseudocode.name: insert(key)
lines: if tree is full and key is new: return overflow error
if root = null: root ← new leaf(key, height 0); return
walk from root: key < node → left, key > node → right
if key = node.value: reject duplicate
attach new leaf(key, height 0) where the walk ended
for each ancestor on the path, bottom-up:
height ← 1 + max(h(left), h(right)); bf ← h(left) − h(right)
if bf = +2 and bf(left) ≥ 0: LL → rotateRight(node)
if bf = +2 and bf(left) < 0: LR → rotateLeft(left), rotateRight(node)
if bf = −2 and bf(right) ≤ 0: RR → rotateLeft(node)
if bf = −2 and bf(right) > 0: RL → rotateRight(right), rotateLeft(node)
if subtree height did not change: stop

pseudocode.name: delete(key)
lines: if root = null: return empty error
walk from root to find key; if missing: return error
if node has ≤ 1 child: link parent to that child (or null)
else: succ ← leftmost node of node.right (in-order successor)
node.value ← succ.value; link succ's parent to succ.right
for each ancestor on the path, bottom-up:
height ← 1 + max(h(left), h(right)); bf ← h(left) − h(right)
if bf = +2 and bf(left) ≥ 0: LL → rotateRight(node)
if bf = +2 and bf(left) < 0: LR → rotateLeft(left), rotateRight(node)
if bf = −2 and bf(right) ≤ 0: RR → rotateLeft(node)
if bf = −2 and bf(right) > 0: RL → rotateRight(right), rotateLeft(node)
if subtree height did not change: stop

pseudocode.name: search(key)
lines: curr ← root
while curr != null
if key == curr.value: return found
if key < curr.value: curr ← curr.left
else: curr ← curr.right
return not found

pseudocode.name: min()
lines: if root == null: return empty error
curr ← root
while curr.left != null: curr ← curr.left
return curr

pseudocode.name: max()
lines: if root == null: return empty error
curr ← root
while curr.right != null: curr ← curr.right
return curr

pseudocode.name: inspect(kind)
lines: root: the one node with no parent
leaf: node.left == null and node.right == null
internal node: has at least one child

pseudocode.name: clear()
lines: unlink all nodes (O(n));  root ← null;  size ← 0

insert.note: BST insert plus bottom-up retracing using an O(log n) ancestor path array. At most one single or double rotation restores balance.

delete.note: Uses the in-order successor for two-child nodes and retraces an O(log n) path array; up to O(log n) rotations may occur.

search.note: Height stays below 1.44·log₂(n + 2). Iterative walk uses O(1) extra space (the visualizer also stores the visited path for display).

min.note: Follows left pointers from the root to the leftmost node.

max.note: Follows right pointers from the root to the rightmost node.

height.note: Reads the height stored on the root node (−1 when empty, 0 for a single leaf).

inspect.note: In-order traversal that collects all nodes matching root, leaves, or internal.

clear.note: Pre-order recursion unlinks every node along an O(log n) call stack.

applications: In-memory ordered dictionaries and sets where lookups vastly outnumber writes, benefiting from AVL's strict height bound.
Database and file-system indexes that need fast range queries, predecessor/successor lookups, and guaranteed O(log n) worst-case reads.
Memory allocators that index free blocks by size to find the best-fitting block in O(log n) time.
Leaderboards and order books that keep dynamic scores or prices sorted while answering min, max, and lookup queries quickly.

misconceptions.mistake: Rotations change the sorted in-order sequence of keys in the tree.
misconceptions.correction: Every single or double rotation preserves the binary search tree invariant. Watch the In-Order Keys strip during any rotation demo: the sorted order of values never changes.

misconceptions.mistake: An AVL tree must be completely symmetric with balance factor 0 at every node.
misconceptions.correction: AVL allows balance factors of −1, 0, and +1. A subtree may be 1 level deeper than its sibling without triggering any rotation; only |bf| = 2 is unbalanced.

misconceptions.mistake: Delete needs at most one rotation, just like insert.
misconceptions.correction: Insert stops after its first rotation case because the subtree returns to its old height. Delete can shrink a rotated subtree's height by 1, causing imbalances higher up and up to O(log n) rotations.

misconceptions.mistake: An empty child has height 0, the same as a leaf.
misconceptions.correction: In the edge-count convention used on this page, a leaf has height 0 and an empty child has height −1. That is why a node with one leaf on the left and nothing on the right has bf = 0 − (−1) = +1.

tryIt.label: Single rotation: Insert LL demo
tryIt.action: Choose “Insert LL: 30, 20 then insert 10” in “Case” and press “Run Demo”. Then press “⏮ Reset” and step through with “Step ▶”.
tryIt.expect: The banner reads “Demo: tree [30, 20], then insert 10. Rotations: LL at 30.” Step 6 flags “[LL case] 30 has balance factor +2 (left-heavy)” and step 7 rotates right around 30 so 20 becomes root with height 1 and bf 0.

tryIt.label: Double rotation: Insert LR demo
tryIt.action: Choose “Insert LR: 30, 10 then insert 20” in “Case” and press “Run Demo”, then watch steps 6 through 9.
tryIt.expect: Step 6 detects “LR case: first rotate 10 left, then rotate 30 right.” Step 7 runs rotation 1 of 2 around 10, step 8 runs rotation 2 of 2 around 30, and step 9 ends with “Rebalanced with 1 rotation case: LR at 30 (20 moved up).”

tryIt.label: Delete triggers an RL double rotation
tryIt.action: Choose “Delete RL: 20, 10, 30, 25 then delete 10” in “Case” and press “Run Demo”.
tryIt.expect: Removing leaf 10 leaves 20 with balance factor −2 and right child 30 with +1. Steps 6 and 7 rotate 30 right then 20 left, ending with “Deleted 10. Rebalanced with 1 rotation case: RL at 20 (25 moved up). The tree has 3 nodes and height 1.”

tryIt.label: Build sorted keys without degenerating
tryIt.action: Type the input in “Values (1–31 unique whole numbers, −99 to 999)” and press “Build”.
tryIt.expect: The banner shows “Built an AVL tree of 7 keys (height 2, 4 rotation cases along the way).” Instead of a height-6 chain like a plain BST, 40 becomes the root and Balanced reads “Yes (every |bf| ≤ 1)”.

tryIt.label: Duplicate rejection and two-child delete
tryIt.action: With that 7-key tree loaded, type 40 in “Value (−99 to 999)” and press “Insert”. Then press “Delete” while 40 is still in the box.
tryIt.expect: Insert is refused with “40 is already in the AVL tree (keys must be unique).” Delete succeeds with “Deleted 40 using in-order successor 50. No rotation needed.” and 50 becomes the new root of the 6-node tree.

tryIt.label: Highlight leaves and internal nodes
tryIt.action: On the remaining 6-node tree, select “Leaf nodes” in “Highlight” and press “Highlight”, then select “Internal (parent) nodes” and press “Highlight”.
tryIt.expect: Leaf nodes reports “Leaves (3): 10, 30, 70.” and Internal nodes reports “Internal nodes (3): 20, 50, 60.” while highlighting each set on the tree stage.
